turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mrs Adeyemi, come through. I've put your weight and blood pressure on the screen for Dr Shah.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, thank you. Sorry, I'm a bit all over the place. Is the pulse on there as well? I was rushing, the lift in the car park was broken.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Yes. Weight seventy-one kilos, blood pressure one hundred and eighteen over seventy-six, pulse ninety-four. I don't interpret them, so mention the pulse to the doctor. She'll call you straight in.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-four. Is that bad? I knew I shouldn't have run up.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): That's one for Dr Shah, love. In you go.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit down. What's the problem today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I've been exhausted, my periods are a nightmare, and I get breathless. My sister made me come, she thinks it's my thyroid, but you ask and I'll try to be quick.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long tired?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Most of this year, it crept up, and afternoons I just want to lie down. I work in a school office and I've been making silly mistakes, which isn't me.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathless at rest or on effort?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): On effort, on the stairs. We're in a maisonette, one flight, and I'm puffed at the top, not when I'm sitting. It's been a couple of months, maybe longer, and I can't pin the day down.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the chest. I googled heart attacks anyway, which I know is stupid. Is breathlessness on its own still dangerous?
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll get there. Periods heavy for how long?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): About a year. They were four or five days before, fine. Now I flood, especially at night. Sorry, it's embarrassing to say out loud.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pads per day?

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I lose count. A bad day, six or seven, maybe more, and I change every couple of hours and still leak. Nights I use the big maternity ones, and I should have written it down.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Clots?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, big ones, about a fifty-pence piece, sometimes bigger, though I don't really know. Most days of the period, not all the time. Does the size matter, and can you actually bleed too much from clots?
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): It means the flow is heavy. Bleeding between periods?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing in between. And no pain really, just the flooding, well, a bit of dragging on day one, low down, but not proper pain.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hair thinning?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, coming out in the shower for a few months, and my ponytail's half what it was. Nails split too. Is that the same as the tiredness, or something else?
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Often the same. On iron?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ferrous sulphate, the other GP gave it ages ago, two hundred milligrams I think the box says. I'm meant to take one a day, but I only take it sometimes, two or three times a week if I remember. It bungs me up, so I skip it.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that awful? Will today's blood test be useless if I had one yesterday? Should I have been stricter?
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not awful, but take one tablet a day from now, with food. Don't stop it for the test. Water helps the constipation, and don't double the dose if you miss one.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): With food, right. Not with tea? I read tea blocks iron. And the constipation, will it be every day if I take it properly? I can't be stuck at work.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not with tea. Water or juice. Any other tablets?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Vitamin D, a thousand units, most mornings, a friend suggested it. Paracetamol if the dragging's annoying, not every day. That's all.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Operations? Other illnesses?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. About six months ago the old surgery did a blood test and they said the haemoglobin was borderline, no number, just borderline, try the iron, and I never went back. Is borderline actual anaemia, because I've had it in my head it's leukaemia, which is ridiculous?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Borderline without a figure isn't usable. We repeat it. This is not a leukaemia story.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. My sister rang last week and said thyroid problems run in our family. Mum's had an underactive thyroid for years and she's on thyroxine. Could it be that and not the iron at all?
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Possible. We'll check it. Not definite.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): She wanted to come in but she's on shift. Do I definitely inherit it? And should I stop the vitamin D in case it muddles the thyroid test?
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not definitely. Don't stop the vitamin D. Weight changed?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit up, maybe half a stone, though I've been snacking because I'm shattered so I'm not sure it means anything. Rings still fit.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, go on.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest clear, no wheeze. Heart sounds normal but a bit quick. Pale, inner eyelids especially, and the tummy is soft with no mass.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Pale means anaemia, doesn't it? And the quick heart, the ninety-four, is that dangerous? I get a thump when I lie down sometimes, and I didn't want to sound dramatic.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): A little fast, fits with rushing and with being short of iron. Not dangerous while you're sitting here.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): The thumping is only some nights, a few seconds, not every night. Should I have led with that? I'm sorry.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blackouts?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've never fainted.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Working impression: the heavy periods are driving an iron deficiency, and that would cover the tiredness, the breathlessness and the hair. Thyroid stays on the list because of your mum. I can't confirm either until the bloods.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): So not cancer? My neighbour had fibroids and a hysterectomy, and I'm only forty-one and I don't want an operation. Are we heading there?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): No surgery talk today. Bloods: full blood count, ferritin, thyroid function, and a clotting screen because of the flooding.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Clotting, so you think my blood doesn't clot? Ferritin is the iron store, isn't it? How many needles?

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ferritin is the store. The clotting screen is routine with flooding this heavy, not because I suspect a clotting disorder. One blood draw, a few small tubes, after we finish.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): And a scan? My sister said I'd need a pelvic scan. Is that today? What if it shows fibroids?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the bleeding stays this heavy, or the bloods don't give us the whole answer, we might arrange a pelvic ultrasound, and it's not booked.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): So I might avoid it. How long for the blood results? I can't sit with this for a month, I'll spiral.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Usually a week. Follow-up here in one week. If you're soaking through more than hourly, or you feel faint, go to A&E and don't wait for me.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Hourly, right. Can I still go to work? I'm frightened I'll pass out at the desk. What do I tell my sister?
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Work is fine. Sit down if you're puffed, and don't charge the stairs. Tell her nothing's confirmed, and reception will book both.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, sorry for the questions, I lie awake going over it. One more, then I'll stop: the iron with orange juice, every single day, even on my period?
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every day, juice or water, including during the period. That's the lot.

[SEG0059] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Bloods this afternoon at four with the phlebotomist, and you're back with Dr Shah in one week. We'll text both times. Bring the iron box if you can, so we can check the strength.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Four is fine. I'll bring the box. Thank you, both of you.

spec.situation: Tired, breathless woman with heavy periods for a year; counts pads and clots in vague terms; takes iron 'sometimes'; hair loss; relative mentions thyroid in the family. Blood tests, maybe pelvic scan.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: Prior blood test with borderline haemoglobin mentioned, but not requested by patient and not stated as completed today.

omissions.text: No other illnesses were reported when asked ('No operations.').
Previous blood test about six months ago at the old surgery was said to show haemoglobin was 'borderline' with no number given, and the patient was advised to try iron but did not go back.
Doctor stated that the prior 'borderline' result without a figure is not usable and said 'This is not a leukaemia story.'
Family history detail missing: patient said her sister reported that thyroid problems run in the family, in addition to mother having an underactive thyroid on thyroxine.
Medication history detail missing: mother is on thyroxine for underactive thyroid.
Negative finding missing: patient said there was 'no pain really' with periods, only mild dragging on day 1, i.e. no significant pelvic pain.
Follow-up logistics missing: blood draw was booked for that afternoon at 4 pm with the phlebotomist, and the patient would be texted both appointment times.
Investigation timing/detail missing: doctor said the blood tests would be done after the consultation in one blood draw using a few small tubes.
Results timing missing: doctor said blood results usually take about a week.
